steps.action:
# The Last Light

Old Marcus had kept the light for thirty-one years. He knew every mood the sea could wear.

On the night the storm came in from the northeast, he climbed the iron stairs for the four-hundredth time that month, his knees arguing with every step. The lantern room was cold. It was always cold in November.

He lit the lamp and watched the beam cut through the dark, slow and steady. One rotation every four seconds. He'd counted them so many times the rhythm lived in his chest like a second heartbeat.

Somewhere out there, a ship was trying to find its way home.

He made coffee on the small gas stove and sat by the window, watching. The waves threw themselves against the rocks below with what he always thought was a kind of passion — reckless and beautiful and not caring at all who was watching.

At 2 a.m., he saw the distant lights of a fishing vessel, too far north, drifting toward the shoals. He watched it for a long minute, his coffee growing cold in his hands.

Then the ship adjusted course.

Just like that.

Marcus nodded once and drank his coffee. He never knew their names, never met the people he'd saved. That was the whole point, he figured. The light didn't ask for anything in return.

It just kept turning.
